failure_modes: Trivial collapse: R^2 near 1 with exponents near 0 because the measure is dominated by density, not structure
Broad exponent confidence intervals spanning zero signal that no scaling relation is present
Narrow density range from short laboratory windows leaves the scaling function poorly constrained
Taking a good collapse as proof of universality when between-sample variance (ICC) is high
gloss: Rescale entropy and density by system size until all samples fall on one curve, then read regimes from the residue
invariants: Entropy and control parameter are both made intensive before fitting
The same ansatz and optimiser are applied to empirical and null data
Exponent uncertainties come from resampling, not from a single fit
mechanism: Samples differ in how many agents or interactions fill the same observation area, so raw entropies mix size with structure. Make both quantities intensive: entropy density eta = H / A_o and control parameter rho = N_V / A_o (agent density for an agent network, interaction-event density for an event network). Take the characteristic system size S = <rho> per sample and fit the finite-size scaling ansatz eta(rho, S) = S^alpha f(rho S^-beta): choose alpha and beta (e.g. by Nelder-Mead) to minimise sum_ij (eta_ij S^-alpha - f(rho_ij S^-beta))^2 over samples i and windows j, and bootstrap windows to get exponent uncertainties. A good collapse means a shared scaling law; systematic, regime-labelled departures from the collapsed curve are the signal. Compare the collapse with the same procedure on {{null_model}} data, and test departures with {{clustered_testing}}. Interpret exponents too: near-zero exponents with a near-perfect fit mean the measure is simply tracking density.
postconditions: Each observation has rescaled coordinates (rho S^-beta, eta S^-alpha) in which regimes can be compared at matched density
preconditions: Observations span a range of densities wide enough to constrain alpha and beta
